# Classroom Debate as a Pedagogical Method to Explore the Relationship Between the Medical System and Patient Community Members

**Authors:** Naeema Hopkins-Kotb; Elizabeth Janiak; Alex S. Keuroghlian; Deborah Bartz

**Affiliations:** 11811Harvard Medical School, Boston, MA, USA | 21861Brigham and Women's Hospital, Boston, MA, USA | 31857Harvard TH Chan School of Public Health, Boston, MA, USA | 42348Massachusetts General Hospital, Boston, MA, USA

## Abstract

There are multiple complexities within the practice of medicine wherein the vantage of the medical community might be limited or in direct conflict with the vantage of a patient population. Reproductive justice (RJ) is a framework developed from the vantage of Black women's health activists to identify and address inequitable reproductive health outcomes, consider the intersection of reproductive rights and social justice, and center the experiences of historically marginalized communities. Using the contemporary example of the federal Medicaid Sterilization Form, we highlight how the pedagogy of classroom debate can teach medical students to engage thoughtfully with the complex intersection between community population perspectives and the medical profession's advocacy for standardized provision of health services. Debate has long-standing use in education and can build core medical student communication and professionalism competencies while facilitating active learning around complex medical care topics. However, it can have limited efficacy without careful attention to the development of a psychologically safe learning environment and the inclusion of nuanced and diverse perspectives. Herein, we share our debate curriculum and demonstrate how this approach aligns with the community-developed RJ framework that recognizes systems outside medicine that contribute to reproductive outcomes. Our method encourages students to critically evaluate existing literature for authorship, representation, and community participation—a crucial practice for all students to understand the importance of equity in medical research development and healthcare.

## Introduction

All medical learners will care for patients deeply affected by inequitable—disparate and unjust—health opportunities and outcomes. This is particularly true when rotating within reproductive health. Maternity care deserts, highly variable state regulations and restrictions, and structural racism all contribute to Black U.S. women suffering from three times greater risk of death in childbirth than White women at all levels of income and education. 1 More than half of these deaths are preventable. 1 Black women also have higher rates of severe maternal morbidity and cervical cancer and lower rates of sexually transmitted infection detection and treatment and human papillomavirus vaccination.2–5

These disparities in U.S. reproductive health outcomes, despite long-standing recognition, are worsening.6–8 Likely, we have been unable to make headway in these disparate health outcomes in part because of the narrow view through which the medical profession views the problem. Medical research, clinical policies, and educational curricula are largely developed by medical and scientific professionals who carry power, privilege, and positionality that limit the vantage through which they investigate, understand, and teach healthcare disparities. Apart from the small discipline of community-based participatory research (CBPR), members of involved populations are rarely included in helping medical professionals understand contributors to health disparities. Modern medical education largely relies on the scientific literature developed for and by medical and scientific professionals. Therefore, the perspectives and understanding of affected community members rarely make their way to learners unless we deliberately seek out these community voices when developing curricula. 9

Reproductive justice (RJ) is a framework developed by Black women's health activists in 1994 to identify and address inequitable reproductive health outcomes by considering the intersection of reproductive health, reproductive rights, and social justice. Critically, RJ relies on centering the experiences of people with marginalized identities. 10 “Nothing about us, without us” is a key tenet of RJ, indicating programmatic development requires inclusion of community members of the population of interest. 9 Furthermore it draws on influences outside the medical system—such as laws, policies, education, economic opportunities, safety, housing, and food security—that affect reproductive health access and outcomes. Within the United States, these influences vary along identity axes of race, gender, sexual orientation, and disability. Therefore, RJ serves as an excellent example framework for medical learners. It allows them to contextualize marginalized perspectives and examine how health disparities and structural racism shape medical practice and clinical outcomes.

Given the differing, and sometimes conflicting, perspectives between medical professionals and community members, we believe debate provides a unique opportunity to highlight this interaction in the medical classroom. A well-developed debate curriculum can effectively elevate patient community voices in student learning. In this report, we describe a novel application of classroom debate as an educational method to ground a contemporary RJ example, engage students in complex critical thinking, and accentuate the value of the voices of an affected community.

## Debate as a Pedagogical Method in Medical Education

Debate is a well-established pedagogical method used for centuries in education. It has ancient origins, dating back to Ancient Greece where Protagoras of Abdera, often called the “father of debate,” first introduced the concept in an educational setting.11–13 It has been employed in medical education in recent decades to help learners engage with complex and controversial clinical scenarios and ethical dilemmas.12,14 Classroom debate is a form of experiential learning where students, through critical analysis and selection of evidence, provide support for an assigned “side” of an issue. 11 Classically, these “sides” are designated as “for” or “against” a particular viewpoint or assertion. However, there can be flexibility in the format used for debate. Debates can involve three or more “sides,” role-play, think-pair-share, and group problem-solving formats, among others. 13

Critics of debate cite concerns about an excessive workload in preparation for debate, a potential for biasing learners toward a black-and-white dualistic mindset, a reinforcement of students’ existing beliefs instead of challenging them to consider nuanced viewpoints, and the development of a confrontational classroom environment that may affect psychological safety.12,13 However, with careful consideration of the preparation time, the classroom culture that is cultivated, and the engagement of the medical learner, debate can be incredibly effective and formative for trainees,15,16 with a resulting resurgence of this pedagogy noted in contemporary undergraduate medical education. 14

When crafted and facilitated well by faculty, classroom debate is a highly effective learning modality that promotes evidence-based investigation, content reinforcement, team communication, public speaking, active listening, critical thinking, learner self-evaluation, as well as affective engagement with the debated topic.12,14,16–18 Debate offers an opportunity to explore a complex topic without resorting to oversimplification or generalization. It has been shown to support adult learning by making students responsible for their learning through active engagement in a problem-centered, experiential approach. 14 These outcomes have also been consistently expressed and appreciated in studies of student perceptions. Students tend to view classroom debate positively and appreciate the development of teamwork skills, confidence, respect for other viewpoints, and a deeper understanding of the debated topic.14,18,19

Overall, classroom debate has significant potential to enrich the learning experience of medical students when designed with careful attention to student workload, nuanced viewpoints, and the laying of respectful classroom ground rules. Moreover, we have found this pedagogical approach can be used to highlight and eliminate gaps in traditional medical education where marginalized patient community voices are missing. Our proposed methodology for a RJ-centered classroom debate aims to build from existing advantages of the debate approach while deliberately creating space for medical trainees to learn, understand, and advocate for the historically marginalized voices previously absent from the medical curriculum.

## Our Model for a Reproductive Justice Debate

### The conflict

We developed a debate surrounding the Federal Medicaid Title XIX Sterilization Consent Form (MSF). The MSF was developed and mandated by Congress in 1976 in response to widespread coercive and involuntary sterilization practices throughout the United States. With few exceptions, the MSF must be signed by publicly insured patients with their doctors 30 days before any female or male sterilization procedure. 20 On one hand, the MSF works as intended: to insert delay and increase the interactions with the healthcare system needed to ensure a sterilization procedure is being undertaken voluntarily and without coercion. Any person on publicly funded insurance has this requirement, affecting hundreds of thousands of economically disenfranchised people each year. 21 Because of this extra layering of protection for patients that hold a great deal of medical skepticism, the RJ community often advocates for the importance and continued use of the MSF protection against the risk of contemporary involuntary sterilizations. 20

On the other hand, the perspective of those from within the medical community is that the MSF creates barriers to timely sterilization and differences in care by insurance status; a patient with private insurance can receive permanent sterilization when desired without delay. In a recent cohort study using the nationally representative 2013 to 2015 National Survey for Family Growth, people with Medicaid were 56% less likely to complete sterilization than those with private insurance. 21 The medical scientific literature, developed almost exclusively by healthcare professionals, has demonstrated concerns regarding the MSF's contribution to high rates of unfilled sterilization requests, lack of improved consent due to poor MSF readability, and limited sterilization access for immigrants and patients under age 21. 20 These two perspectives generate a tension involving long-standing medical mistrust, medical paternalism, and good medical intentions to eliminate healthcare disparities and honor patient autonomy.

### The learners

Advanced undergraduate medical students enrolled in a four-week selective course dedicated to sex- and gender-informed medicine, were assigned a position to argue. To avoid the two-sided, black-and-white perspective argued by critics of debate, we organized students into three groups. Group A argued for repeal of the MSF and waiting period, Group B argued against repeal, and Group C recommended a policy replacement that considers protections for vulnerable communities while minimizing over-regulation and disparities in access and health care delivery. Groups, with about 8 students, were provided with position statements and relevant literature to support their position as a starting point for further research (Supplement). Students were asked to note the literature's authorship and the identities of the primary voices supporting their position. To date, we have run this activity with four class cohorts of up to 25 students each.

### The intervention

Students were alerted to the debate requirements, the guiding materials (Supplement), and the random group assignments on the first day of the course in a course orientation, giving them close to four weeks to prepare. Student groups met individually over the month to brainstorm their approach, read the relevant literature, and plan their presentations. On the day of the debate, faculty provided an introduction, and each group had 10 minutes to present their argument, with 5 minutes of questions from students in other groups or faculty. Group C heard arguments from both sides and often incorporated new supporting content into their previously developed consensus-building solutions. At the time of the presentation, an entire group stood before the class and worked collaboratively, with each student leading one portion of their group's position. Students had flexibility in presentation style; most used visual aids, case stories of affected individuals, and literature, both scientific and community-developed, to help argue their position. The class discussion concluded with a large group debrief on the positions as a whole, highlighting challenges students encountered researching and arguing their positions, the author voices of the literature they relied on, and questions generated by the debate. The faculty asked questions to the individual groups, and the class as a whole, to help highlight the limitations in the students’ stance in the argument in a supportive and encouraging way.

Students often resort to a position of compromise to resolve the weaknesses of their assigned position's arguments. By assigning a separate group, students in Groups A and B were required to think about the strengths of their position's arguments independently. Group C provided a logical conclusion to the debate by identifying areas of compromise, unification, and improvement surrounding sterilization regulation. They addressed the complexity and nuance of the MSF issue as a whole, considering the feasibility of an improved policy that would protect vulnerable patients while also not setting their healthcare apart as different from those with private insurance.

## RJ Debate Aligns with Key Medical Student Learning Objectives

In a curriculum development study, a panel of varied RJ experts determined through the Delphi method that a RJ-specific medical curriculum should address 11 domains: (a) historical injustices, (b) RJ definitions, (c) oppression, power and bias training, (d) contemporary law and policy, (e) healthcare access, disparities, and structural competency, (f) cultural safety, (g) LGBTQI health, (h) reproductive health, (i) patient care, (j) approaches to reproductive healthcare, and (k) advocacy training. 9 The alignment of RJ learning domains relevant to the debate, with the Accreditation Council for Graduate Medical Education (ACGME) core educational competencies for medical students is shown in Table 1. 9

Our debate format aligns closely with these RJ curriculum learning objectives. 9 In the context of the MSF, students were able to consider historical injustices to patients of color and debate the merits of a contemporary policy. In preparation for the debate, they learned how the MSF affects access to safe sterilization and can create disparities in reproductive health outcomes along axes of identity. Through the process of debate itself, they learned how to present evidence supporting their viewpoint and amplify the perspectives of the communities they represented—a crucial skill for advocacy work.

The debate format itself allows students to practice skills likely transferable to the ACGME core competencies of interpersonal and communication skills, professionalism, systems-based practice, and practice-based learning and improvement. 9 We anticipate students can also use these skills to critically evaluate other health disparities that require a dualistic lens from both the medical community and the patient population perspective.

## Conclusion

Today, within the United States, the practice of medicine is impacted by geographic, political, and regulatory contexts. While reproductive health provision and education serve as important examples, especially after the fall of Roe v. Wade, the debate approach could apply to other complex and disparity-driven topics in medicine, including religious exemptions, medical ethics, and the use of artificial intelligence in healthcare.

The debate format allowed flexibility for sharing clinical cases and discussion reaching a depth appropriate to the students’ experience level. When presented with a contentious topic, students may favor one dominant perspective—either because it is the current practice, supported by field experts, or aligns with the ideological viewpoints of their mentors, course directors, and learning environment. This can lead to anchoring and bias in students’ understanding that would go unchecked without a teaching format encouraging them to interrogate multiple viewpoints.

We encourage medical educators to utilize debate in curriculum planning, especially for nuanced, complex medical care delivery. It will be important to incorporate space for student reflection on the experience of arguing positions they may disagree with and the impact of their varied lived experiences, both of which are important for the professional growth and learning process, especially in values-based medical decision making. We recognize that productive debate only occurs when students feel psychologically safe and adequately prepared to discuss these often emotionally valenced topics. Future application of debate strategies must be coupled with establishing classroom norms to foster these safe spaces, as well as formal impact evaluation of student learning.

Medical students frequently engage with scholarly literature as part of their learning and are rarely provided with or seek out community-based writing outside of the peer-reviewed literature. The practice of examining the authorship and viewpoints represented in this research and writing applies to every domain of their training and will help students both recognize and advocate for the communities whose voices are historically silent.

## Glossary

Reproductive justice (RJ): A framework developed by 14 Black women health activists to identify and address inequitable reproductive health outcomes by considering the intersection of reproductive rights and social justice and centering the experiences of people of marginalized identities. The three core values of RJ include (a) the right to have a child, (b) the right to not have a child, and (c) the right to parent a child in safe and healthy environments.

Female sterilization: A surgical procedure performed to permanently prevent pregnancy, most commonly through ligation of Fallopian tubes.

Medicaid Sterilization Form (MSF): The Federal Medicaid Title XIX Sterilization Consent Form was developed and mandated by Congress in 1976 to protect against involuntary sterilization practices in the United States. For male and female patients with Medicaid insurance, the MSF must be signed 30 days in advance of any sterilization procedure in every state. An exception is made for cases of emergency, requiring the form to be signed at least 72 hours in advance of the sterilization procedure. A common example of cases that fall within emergency exemption are preterm deliveries where sterilization was planned for the same hospitalization as the delivery, but the delivery occurred before the 30-day requirement was reached.

Abstract Background  Stigma is a key barrier to compassionate primary health care delivery and people-centered care (PCC), but is understudied among primary care providers (PCPs). Hepatitis B and C have a significant burden of disease in the Philippines, where there is limited awareness of and access to screening and treatment. Patient-reported stigma has been identified as a significant barrier to hepatitis care in the Philippines, but PCP stigma-related attitudes and behaviors have not been explored in this context. Methods  In this study, we assessed primary PCP-reported stigma-related attitudes and behaviors toward patients with hepatitis B and C. We surveyed primary PCPs in Tarlac, Philippines working within a network of healthcare facilities that have been part of an initiative to decentralize hepatitis care to the primary care level and prioritize PCC. Results  We found that PCPs’ self-reported attitudes toward patients with hepatitis B and C reflect a strong sense of responsibility to provide care, and comfort with sensitive history-taking, but also pervasive attitudes of pity and blame. PCPs’ self-reported behaviors showed commitment to providing equal care, but variation in infection control practices suggesting misconceptions about transmission risk. Conclusions  Our results provide essential insight into PCPs’ stigma-related attitudes and behaviors that will serve as a baseline for future comparison with patient-reported experiences. These findings underscore the critical role of primary care in addressing stigma and improving hepatitis care in the Philippines, highlighting the importance of training, resource allocation, and people-centered care strategies. Background Primary health care (PHC) has been well-established as a cornerstone approach for achieving universal health coverage (UHC) [1, 2]. People-centered care (PCC) has emerged alongside PHC as a necessary component to ensure access to quality care for all. PCC is a multi-fac­ eted approach that respects the social context – families, communities, populations – in which individuals access care [3–5]. It also orients individuals’ needs, values, and preferences over their life course at the forefront of their care. A key component of this holistic approach includes fostering a compassionate and supportive care environ­ ment between care providers and patients that functions in tandem with developing a strong primary care work­ force [4, 6]. Ultimately, the goal of PCC is to achieve the right care, at the right time, in the right place, with the right team, in the right way. For this reason, people-cen­ tered models of care can support primary health careoriented health system design and improvement, and the goal of UHC.

With compassion as a driving force of providing pri­ mary healthcare the “right way,” its absence in healthcare can lead to discrimination and poor experiences of care as a result of stigma [7]. Compassion has a myriad of positive effects not only on the physical and mental wellbeing of patients and their providers, but also in driving health services design and delivery that is aligned with community needs [7, 8]. In 2024, the WHO released a report on compassion and PHC, citing that “social, cul­ tural or economic distance from those suffering can lead to misunderstanding, bias and stigmatization” [8]. While this distance, and the resulting stigmatization, are key barriers to compassionate primary healthcare, there is limited literature regarding stigma in the PHC context, especially among primary care providers (PCPs) [9–11].

Here, we use a disease-specific example to study PCPs’ stigma-related attitudes and behaviors in the care of patients with hepatitis B (HBV) and C (HCV) in the Phil­ ippines. We define stigma in this context to describe neg­ ative stereotypes or social disapproval directed toward individuals based on their hepatitis status. HBV and HCV are endemic to the Philippines and contribute to avoid­ able mortality [12, 13]. The viruses can be transmitted via blood, sexual contact, unsterile needles from intra­ venous drug use, tattoo, or piercing practices, accidental needlestick injuries (especially in healthcare settings), unsterile medical or dental procedures, and perinatally. There remain many barriers to accessing and delivering hepatitis screening and treatment in the Philippines, with a recent patient journey mapping study identifying a vari­ ety of barriers across the course of patients’ journeys in seeking care, including fear of stigma and discrimination [14].

In this study, we surveyed the attitudes and behaviors of PCPs working at primary care sites under an initiative to decentralize hepatitis care to the primary care level in Tarlac, Philippines. Tarlac has been a focus region of recent governmental efforts to decentralize hepatitis care to the primary care level, aiming to address barriers and provide person-centered care. Our study captured PCPs who care for patients with HBV and HCV, most of whom have undergone training on PCC for people with hepati­ tis as a part of this initiative [15].

Methods This study utilized a quantitative 40-question anonymous survey administered online via RedCap. The survey had three parts: (1) attitudes related to hepatitis care provi­ sion (9 questions) (2), behaviors related to hepatitis care provision (8 questions), and (3) demographic information (8 questions). Questions in parts 1 and 2 were primar­ ily composed of 5-pt Likert scale (strongly disagree, dis­ agree, uncertain, agree, strongly agree) questions asking respondents to indicate the extent to which they agreed with the listed statements.

Since there are no previously-validated tools to assess hepatitis-related stigma in the Philippine context, parts 1 and 2 questions were developed based on prior stud­ ies assessing provider attitudes and behaviors related to hepatitis and HIV care provision from other contexts. Specifically, questions asking about comfort with, and responsibility for, sexual history-taking were adapted from the Healthcare Provider HIV/AIDS Stigma Scale [16]. All other attitude and behavior questions were adapted from Richmond et al. study of health profes­ sionals’ attitudes toward patients with hepatitis C [17, 18]. See Supplement for survey questions (S1). To evalu­ ate provider attitudes surrounding feelings of pity, shame or judgment in the care of patients with hepatitis, PCPs were asked to what extent they agree that people who inject drugs deserve to be infected with HBV/HCV, that they feel sorry for people who contracted HBV/HCV, and that they feel judged or shamed by others for providing care and treatment to patients with HBV/HCV. We also assessed provider comfort with taking a patient history about sensitive topics related to hepatitis transmission (substance use, sex) and their sense of responsibility for the care of patients with HBV/HCV. To evaluate pro­ vider behaviors, we asked about providing the same stan­ dard of care, avoiding transmission of HBV/HCV from their patients to others, and following infection control guidelines.

All questions were reviewed and edited by Filipino researchers familiar with care provision in the Philippines to ensure they were context-appropriate. Part 3 questions asked for standard demographic information, including context of caring for patients with hepatitis, estimated

The study was approved by the Mass General Brigham Institutional Review Board and the University of the Phil­ ippines Manila Research Ethics Board. Survey questions were translated from English to Tagalog and respondents were able to select their preferred language in RedCap before completing the survey. All patients consented to the survey by providing an electronic signature at the start of the survey. Survey respondents received 500 PHP (approximately 8.5 USD) via G-Cash (a local Filipino mobile payment platform) for the completion of the sur­ vey. The survey was administered during telementoring sessions with providers and was otherwise circulated in informal networks (Messenger, Facebook, WhatsApp) amongst providers working at seven care facilities (TPH Cares, Concepcion Tambayan, Concepcion RHU 1, Con­ cepcion RHU 2, Concepcion RHU 3, Moncada RHU 1, Moncada RHU 2) in Tarlac, Philippines between August- November 2024. Based on estimates of the number of providers involved in hepatitis care decentralization across these facilities, the target number of respondents was 30–40 PCPs. Partial survey responses were not included. “Agree/strongly agree” and “disagree/strongly disagree” Likert responses were combined to represent “Agree” and “Disagree” for the purposes of data analysis.

Results A total of 30 PCPs completed the entire survey (Table 1). All seven Tarlac healthcare facilities were represented. The majority of respondents were female (83%), nurses

(40%), and had received training/telementoring in the past 12 months (80%). The average age of respondents was 42.

Provider attitudes related to people living with hepatitis B/C When asked if they feel sorry for individuals who have contracted HBV/HCV, 26% (8/30) indicated they did not (Fig. 1). Almost a third of respondents (30%, 9/30) agreed with the statement that people who inject drugs deserve to be infected with hepatitis B or C (Fig. 1). Similarly, 26% (8/30) did not feel sympathy for individuals who have contracted HBV/HCV (Fig. 1). Judgment or shame from others for providing care and treatment to patients with hepatitis B or C was reported by 23% (7/30) of respon­ dents (Fig.  1). A majority of providers expressed com­ fort with discussing sensitive topics with their patients. Talking about sexual practices was comfortable for 70% (21/30) of respondents, while 73% (22/30) felt at ease dis­ cussing injection drug use practices (Fig. 1).

Most providers recognized their role in patient educa­ tion and treatment. Counseling patients about safe sexual practices was seen as a responsibility by 77% (23/30) of respondents (Fig.  1). Willingness to treat people with HBV/HCV was reported by 93% (28/30), and nearly all providers (97%, 29/30) believed their profession should play a central role in the treatment of hepatitis B and C (Fig.  1). Most respondents (80%, 24/30) also indicated that they would get in trouble at work if they discrimi­ nated against a person living with hepatitis B or C (Fig. 1).

Provider behaviors related to people living with hepatitis B/C The majority of providers (92%, 22/24) indicated that they deliver the same standard of care to patients with HBV/HCV as they do for others (Fig.  2). A substantial portion (69%, 20/29) agreed that identifying patients with hepatitis B or C is necessary to protect the care team from transmission (Fig.  2). While 38% (11/29) believed that patients with hepatitis B or C should be given the last appointment of the day to prevent transmission to others, 62% (18/29) disagreed with this practice (Fig. 2). Concerns about transmission through contact with clothing, bedding, or belongings of affected patients were expressed by 21% (6/29) of respondents (Fig. 2).

A significant proportion (78%, 21/27) agreed that all patients should be tested for HBV/HCV before under­ going invasive procedures (Fig.  2). The preference for using two pairs of gloves when treating a bleeding person with HBV/HCV was reported by 73% (19/26) of provid­ ers (Fig. 2). Additionally, 81% (21/26) indicated that they frequently implement extra infection control precautions when treating these patients (Fig. 2). Discussion Attitudes PCPs indicated strong attitudes of responsibility for hep­ atitis care. However, responses were notably more mixed around counseling and history-taking for intravenous drug use and sexual practices. Notably, 20% were uncer­ tain about history-taking for injection drug use and 20% were uncomfortable counseling on safe sex. There is a potential underlying training gap needed for PCPs to feel comfortable with these sensitive and highly stigmatized subject areas that are central to preventing transmis­ sion of HBV/HCV. While most respondents indicated an absence of directed stigmatizing actions toward patients with hepatitis, a significant minority reported internal­ ized stigmatizing attitudes like pity and blame. These may

be linked to prevailing attitudes toward people who use drugs in the Philippines, including that drug addiction is a sign of moral or character weakness or lack of will to stop [19, 20].

Our findings are consistent with the Filipino context and limited studies in the Southeast Asian region. One study found that Vietnamese physicians caring for female sex workers reported less thorough sexual history-taking than physicians in the United States, United Kingdom, and Australia due to patient and physician discomfort with the subject [21]. Additionally, the historical presence of severely punitive drug laws, judicial and extrajudicial killing for drug use in the Philippines may contribute to the stigmatization of intravenous drug use and is likely a forcible contributor to fear and discomfort around dis­ cussing the topic in the clinical setting [22, 23]. A Filipino household survey on drug abuse found that health prob­ lems were the most cited negative effect of drug use, with

Given the prevailing pressures around judgment affecting care for hepatitis patients, it will be important to engage PCPs in continuing educa­ tion about how co-stigmatizing risk factors, like sex and drug use, affect care provision.

Behaviors Almost all PCPs indicated they provide the same stan­ dard of care to patients with and without HBV/HCV, suggesting a reassuring alignment between PCP beliefs and practice. Responses were more mixed when provid­ ers were asked about behaviors that effectively “single out” patients with HBV/HCV, including identifying them to protect the care team and giving them the last appointment of the day to prevent transmission to other patients. While intended to prevent transmission, these practices exemplify structural stigma by systematically marginalizing patients through the denial of privacy and reduced accessibility within the healthcare system. In the health setting, structural stigma operates through insti­ tutional policies that reinforce exclusion and inequitable healthcare access, shaping not only patient experiences but also provider attitudes and behaviors [25]. Hospital policies and practices like these have historically singled out HBV and HCV (along with HIV), potentially over­ estimating transmission risks and being driven more by stigma-related fears and anxieties than by evidence-based assessments. This reflects broader societal conditions and institutional norms that constrain opportunities, resources, and the well-being of stigmatized individu­ als. Similarly, a significant minority of PCPs worried about HBV/HCV transmission through touching patient belongings. Despite most surveyed PCPs having received training on the prevention, and transmission of HBV/ HCV, this finding reflects a persistent knowledge and/ or practice gap that should be a focus of future training efforts.

The majority of respondents agreed with testing for HBV/HCV before invasive procedures, double-gloving when handling blood, and using additional infection con­ trol precautions. WHO recommendations for preventing HBV/HCV infection include hand hygiene, safe handling of waste/sharps, equipment cleaning, testing donated blood, improving access to safe blood, and health per­ sonnel training, but do not indicate specific protocols for these guidelines [26]. Basic infection prevention and control guidelines are set by the Department of Health in the Philippines, serving as a foundation for hospitalspecific protocols [27]. PCPs can decide the extent of personal protective equipment and practices they use, introducing variation in practice that may not be evi­ dence-based. Current evidence is insufficient to suggest

double gloving significantly prevents transmission of blood-borne viruses [28]. Extra prevention efforts may reflect an effort by PCPs to protect themselves, suggest­ ing a fear of HBV/HCV that may consciously or subcon­ sciously drive stigmatizing practices. Future studies will be needed to elucidate the motivations behind these per­ sonal protective choices.

Stigma as a systems-level barrier to PCC Stigma has commonly been studied from a disease-spe­ cific lens but can, and should, be studied as a systemslevel barrier of compassionate care [29, 30]. PCPs care for patients across multiple communicable (HIV, hepati­ tis, respiratory viral illness etc.) and non-communicable (obesity, diabetes, smoking-related lung diseases, etc.) disease processes that may be afflicted by stigmatizing attitudes and behaviors leading to negative health out­ comes [11, 30]. Additionally, PCPs face multiple pres­ sures including increased provider workload, inadequate provider compensation, and worker shortages, poten­ tially contributing to job stress and burnout which is common among PCPs in LMICs [31, 32]. The effect of these burdens on worsening stigmatizing attitudes and behaviors should be further investigated. Future studies will be necessary to explore how programs can build sup­ portive environments and clinical mentorship that miti­ gate added job stress from care delivery interventions.

Limitations Our study has several limitations. First, the study is likely subject to interviewer and conformity bias as sur­ vey administration occurred during or directly follow­ ing PCC training sessions with the research team. This led to our survey primarily capturing trained PCPs and may have led them to answer more favorably. Second, our sample of PCPs is small and though capturing healthcare facilities across Tarlac, likely limited in generalizability to other providers across the Philippines. Our sample of surveyed PCPs is also mostly concordant with data on the composition of the primary care workforce in the Philippines and internationally. Of note, female nurses were most represented in our sample, and BHWs were underrepresented compared to national estimates [33]. We are also capturing a small sample of providers who haven’t received PCC training. This untrained population of PCPs may be an important future comparator group to evaluate stigma. Additionally, this study adapted sur­ vey questions validated in other contexts. There remains a need for validated context-appropriate tools to study hepatitis-related stigma in the Philippines and the broader Southeast Asian region where the prevalence of chronic viral hepatitis is high. Future development of these tools should prioritize the lens of primary care

Conclusions This survey of Filipino PCPs is the first, to our knowl­ edge, to survey their attitudes and behaviors toward patients with HBV/HCV. PCP attitudes reflect a strong commitment to equal, non-discriminatory care for patients. However, a significant minority hold stigmatiz­ ing attitudes that may reflect the history of criminaliza­ tion of drug use in the Philippines. Though these laws have since changed, they leave a legacy that warrants future study, especially in the primary care context. PCPs in the Philippines also practice infection control behav­ iors that may single out HBV/HCV patients, reflecting structural stigma and resulting in non-evidence-based choices around personal protection in the healthcare set­ ting. This variation in practice may reflect a need for fur­ ther standardization of infection control practices across institutions and especially for stigmatized diseases like hepatitis. Overall, our study provides initial insight into stigma at the PHC level in the Philippines. Promoting compassionate PHC by addressing stigma at a systemic level is essential for achieving UHC, ensuring that all patients– regardless of their condition– receive equita­ ble, evidence-based, and non-discriminatory care.

## ABSTRACT

China’s technological progress in recent decades has been viewed with admiration, alarm, and (in some cases) doubt. To better understand the Chinese innovation ecosystem, we compile a dataset of almost 14 million domestic Chinese patent publications. We focus on the subset of critical technologies identified by the U.S. Department of Defense. Several surprising patterns emerge from the data: Chinese patenting is strongly associated with other measures of innovative progress; patents are not concentrated in corporate giants such as Huawei; universities have played a key role in innovation, much greater than state-owned enterprises or government-owned facilities; and fewer than one in ten Chinese critical technology patents involves an inventor with U.S. experience or training. Finally, using four text-based measures of patent quality, we show that the rise of Chinese patenting in critical technologies has not been associated with a decline in quality relative to the U.S. awards.

## 1 Introduction

Technological innovation in China by almost any measure has surged in recent decades.

Domestic patent publications are one example: they increased from roughly 30,000 annually in 2000 to 1.85 million in 2022, when they exceeded U.S. patent counts by nearly a factor of three. Looking specifically at the 14 Critical Technology Areas designated by the U.S. Department of Defense (DoD), annual Chinese patent publications rose from fewer than 10,000 in the early 2000s to more than 400,000 by 2022. Figure 1 presents these trends.1

The interpretation of the rise of Chinese innovation, however, has been controversial. A number of analysts have claimed that the commonly used innovation indicators overstate Chinese progress. In the context of patents, critics have pointed to the powerful incentives that exist for Chinese entities to undertake patent filings and the very low share of these

filings that are also filed overseas (Li, 2012; Eberhardt et al., 2017). More generally, questions have been raised about the extent to which innovations have truly originated in China, as

opposed to being results of intellectual property misappropriation and/or skilled immigration

from Western nations.2 Academic work has reinforced these concerns, showing, for instance, that Chinese total factor productivity (TFP) growth slowed substantially during the 2010s, even as other innovation metrics accelerated (Wei et al., 2017).

Others point to instances of the dramatic Chinese technological progress. In January 2025,

for instance, the Chinese firm DeepSeek released its R1 large language model, which was then

believed to approach the performance of leading U.S. models at substantially lower cost and compute intensity. The release was widely described as a “Sputnik moment” for American technological leadership.3 Similar reactions followed China’s 2021 test of a nuclear-capable hypersonic missile, which reportedly surprised U.S. intelligence agencies and was described by General Mark Milley as “close to” a Sputnik moment.4 These episodes have supported positive assessments of China’s innovative capacity.

This paper seeks to understand use patent data—a detailed if imperfect measure of

innovation—to understand the Chinese innovative ecosystem. The data reveal an innovation

This paper examines five frequently articulated perceptions about Chinese innovation. We first address the observation that China’s patent explosion coincided with weak TFP

growth, raising concerns that Chinese patents reflected only incremental innovation. We find

that quality-weighted Chinese patenting is strongly correlated with independent measures of scientific output within technology areas, suggesting that patent counts contain meaningful information about underlying innovative activity. Moreover, although aggregate Chinese patent counts are extremely large, they are less unusual when scaled by the size of China’s science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) workforce.

The second relates to the role of large firms. Chinese patents, even in frontier technologies, are not dominated by a handful of giants like Huawei. In fact, innovation activity in China is considerably less concentrated among large firms than in the United States. The top-ten assignee share in Chinese critical technologies declined from roughly ten percent in the late 1990s to four percent by 2022, substantially below the U.S. level of roughly 20 percent.

The third perception concerns the direct involvement of the Chinese government in the production of innovation. (We do not consider subsidies and other incentives.) State-owned

enterprises and the government together account for less than four percent of Chinese critical

We then address a fourth belief, which highlights the role of returnees from the U.S. in Chinese innovation. We find little evidence that Chinese innovation is primarily driven by U.S.-trained returnees. 2021), the construction of international patent families (Putnam, 1997), the disambiguation of

### 2.1 Identifying Critical Technologies

An important aspect of our analysis is that we document these patterns not only for the full universe of Chinese patents, but also separately across 14 critical technologies. ### 3.2 Belief 2: Chinese patenting is dominated by a few giants

Much of the U.S. policy discussions and actions motivated by Chinese innovation have

focused on the very largest firms. Analysts have argued that these Chinese national champion

firms, such as Huawei, Semiconductor Manufacturing International Corporation, and Tencent,

are deeply intertwined with the industrial and economic security goals of the Chinese Communist Party and benefit from massive public subsidies and other favorable treatment (see, for

instance, Thiessen (2024) and Shatz and Egel (2025)). Many of the U.S. government’s efforts to limit knowledge flows to China, such as the Entity List, have focused on these firms.

The data suggest, however, that concentration in Chinese critical technology patents is low and has declined substantially over time. The Chinese top-ten assignee share peaked at

roughly 10 to 11 percent in the late 1990s and mid-2000s before falling to approximately four

percent by 2022; the top-50 share peaked near 26 percent in 2004 and declined to roughly 13 percent by the end of the sample (Figure 3).

By contrast, U.S. critical technology patents have remained considerably more concentrated throughout the period. The U.S. top-ten share has remained close to 20 percent, while the top-50 share has fluctuated within a relatively narrow range between 37 and 41 percent.

### 3.3 Belief 3: Chinese critical technology innovation is primarily

## produced through direct state ownership

Many of the policy discussions about Chinese innovation have highlighted the role of state-owned enterprises and government bodies such as the Peoples Liberation Army. We therefore look at who is filing critical technology patents, with the caveat that we can only

look at direct patent assignments, and not the myriad of formal and informal incentives that the parties may have received (Fang et al., 2025; Banares-Sanchez et al., 2026).

We find that Chinese critical technology patenting is dominated by private firms and universities, rather than by state-owned enterprises. Private firms account for 58.3 percent of cumulative Chinese critical technology patents, while public universities account for 26.6 percent. By contrast, state-owned enterprises and the government together account for less

than four percent of cumulative patenting activity. The remainder is attributable to hospitals, individual inventors, government-affiliated nonprofits, and unclassified entities.

*Figure 4 reports the evolution of the annual patent flow by assignee type. The two dominant sectors—private firms and universities—expand together throughout the sample period. By*

2022, private firms account for approximately 56 percent of annual Chinese critical technology patents and universities for roughly 32 percent. Huawei is the single largest private-sector

assignee. Within the university sector, the seven universities administered by the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology—the “Seven Sons of National Defense”—account for 2.1 percent of cumulative patenting activity.

The university share is the clearest point of divergence between the Chinese and U.S. innovation systems. In China, universities account for 26.6 percent of cumulative critical

In the United States, the corresponding shares are 3.3 percent of critical technology patents

and 4.4 percent of overall domestic patents (Table A.2). U.S. universities therefore represent a relatively small and stable share of patenting activity both within and outside critical

technologies. The cross-country difference in university critical technology patenting—a 26.6 percent share in China versus 3.3 percent in the United States—is approximately eightfold. U.S. critical technology patenting remains overwhelmingly corporate, with firms accounting for 94.9 percent of cumulative patents. IBM, the largest assignee, has 33,322 patents.

The organizational structure of Chinese patents reflects a distinctive role of its higher-

education sector. In Figure A.10, we show that universities are important across all individual

critical technologies but with significant heterogeneity. Biotechnology and AI patents have a larger share of university assignees than others; Human Machine Interfaces and Renewable Energy have much smaller shares of university patents.

This institutional structure is consistent with longstanding Chinese industrial and science policy. The 1996 Law on Promoting the Transformation of Scientific and Technological Achievements, substantially revised in 2015, granted universities expanded autonomy to license and transfer intellectual property arising from publicly funded research and required that researchers receive at least 50 percent of commercialization income. These reforms

complemented other coordination mechanisms, including the establishment of more than 100

nationally designated university science parks and the 2011 Collaborative Innovation Centers initiative.

Taken together, the organizational composition and concentration evidence describe a

Chinese critical technology patent system dominated by private firms and public universities,

with a small direct role for government or state-owned enterprises. Relative to the U.S., the

Chinese system is also substantially less concentrated and characterized by a broader base. The

state’s role therefore appears primarily coordinative rather than directly productive: inventive activity is shaped through institutional mechanisms—most notably the higher-education

system, technology-transfer institutions, public incentive schemes, and procurement priorities— rather than through state ownership of the principal patent-producing organizations.

Several factors complicate interpretation of these late-sample dynamics. The COVID-19 pandemic substantially disrupted international mobility, the China Initiative and expanded exportcontrol restrictions altered the institutional environment governing U.S.–China scientific collaboration, and inventors may have become less willing to disclose foreign affiliations in public professional profiles after 2019. In addition, recent patent cohorts are mechanically

## 4 Conclusion

Patents, while an imperfect measure, have long been used to understand innovation in

Western nations. In this paper, we use Chinese domestic awards to shed light on the Chinese innovative ecosystem.

firms and public universities rather than state-owned enterprises, with universities playing a

far larger role than in the United States. Also distinct from the United States is the low overall

share of large firms. Direct foreign inventor linkages remain limited: fewer than ten percent of

Chinese critical technology patents involve inventors with U.S. training or employment, while

## A.1 The Chinese Patent System

The modern Chinese patent law was enacted at the 4th Meeting of the Standing Committee of the Sixth National People’s Congress on March 12, 1984 (https://english.cnipa.gov. cn/col/col3068/index.html). The founders of the People’s Republic had envisioned a

patent system more than three decades earlier, but the earlier system was quickly abandoned due to the perceived incompatibility of patents and socialism (Cheng, 2023).

Article 22 of the Patent Law of China requires that inventions and utility models for which patent rights are to be granted shall be ones that are novel, creative, and of practical

use. These tests are roughly akin to the notions of novelty, non-obviousness, and enablement articulated in U.S. patent law (35 U.S.C. §101-103). In particular, the creativity criteria

resemble the tests used to determine obviousness in Graham v. John Deere (383 U.S. 1, 17–18 (1966)).

Even in light of these changes, it is natural to be concerned that Chinese patents are very

different from those granted in other nations. For instance, were the scope of Chinese awards very narrow, as has been documented to characterize historical Japanese patents, the high counts of awards might be illusionary.

To examine this question, we proceed in two ways. The first approach is to look at the claims in all patents (regardless if awarded to domestic or foreign assignees) issued in the two nations. We focus on the number of words in the claims section. Appendix Figure A.11

presents this comparison for all patent publications between 1985 and 2021. We see that the relative length of the claims section in Chinese and U.S. patents have remained consistent,

with the Chinese claims sections about 20% shorter than the U.S. ones. There is no evidence of dramatic shifts in claims from this analysis.

The second approach was to interview a number of patent attorneys who has expertise in working with Chinese firms and CNIPA. They highlighted in their conversations several points:

• In its formal structure, the Chinese patent system is modeled after the European patent system, and thus quite similar to the U.S. on many dimensions. In the past decade in

particular, the Chinese government has espoused that a well-operating patent system is

strongly linked to technological progress.

• Chinese firms were initially quite unsophisticated about patents, seeking to maximize the amount of awards, reflecting the incentives introduced by innovation tax credits,

corporate schemes, or pressures from provincial or local authorities to boost patenting. Firms frequently sought to minimize the costs associated with filing, even if it meant foregoing opportunities to obtain broader patents by redrafting applications. Many of the resulting patents were narrow ones that were relatively easy to invent around.

• Over the course of the second half of the 2010 and early 2020s, Chinese firms have

become more sophisticated in understanding the importance of effective claim drafting

and patent prosecution. As a result of this growing awareness, firms have placed greater emphasis on obtaining broader claims, often through repeated rounds of interactions with CNIPA while pursuing an award.

• Many of the same differences in patenting across fields seen in the U.S. are apparent in China as well, with biotechnology firms seeking broad protection and information

technology firms filing large number of awards that may be more helpful when negotiating standards-based patent pools and cross-licensing.

## B.2 Assigning a Primary Patent Class to Chinese Patents

The USPTO clearly delineates a primary technology class for each patent. These originally

used the U.S. Patent Classification scheme, which was a highly idiosyncratic and non-nested

scheme. The bulk of the world’s patent offices, including CNIPA, used the World Intellectual Property Organization’s International Patent Classification scheme, which had about 600 subclasses (e.g., A61K or G06F).

Between 2011 and 2015, the USPTO transitioned to the Combined Patent Classification

scheme, jointly developed by the EPO and the USPTO. The scheme mirrors exactly the IPC at the patent subclass level (apart from class Y02). Much of the recent research using U.S. patents has employed the primary CPC classification (which PatentsView has backfilled for earlier patents).

In Chinese patents, one or more patent classes (using the IPC scheme) are indicated at

the top of the patent, with the first one often indicated in bold. In some cases, multiple IPC classes are indicated in bold. There is no documentation that we are aware of that suggests the CNIPA makes a designation akin to the USPTO’s primary class.

In all our Chinese patent datasets (EPO, CNIPA, and Google), we observe multiple IPC

codes for each patent without any primary code being tagged. To be consistent in assigning a

primary IPC code to each patent, we take the modal four-digit IPC class as the primary class. When there are multiple modal classes, we choose one at random.

## B.3 Distance to the Frontier

We are interested in measuring how far American and Chinese patents are from the global scientific frontier. We define the frontier as the set of top-cited scientific publications

within field-year cells and embed both patents and scientific publications in a shared semantic space. Distance to the frontier is then measured by the proximity of each patent to frontier

publications, allowing us to map each invention to the frontier year it most closely resembles. This yields a transparent measure of “science lag,” defined as the gap between the patent’s

grant year and the frontier year it is closest to. Unlike prior work, which relies on productivity

or citation networks, our approach captures the content-based alignment between technological innovation and the evolving scientific frontier.

Formally, define the scientific frontier Fk,t as the set of scientific publications in field k and year t that lie in the top 10% of the forward citation distribution within (k, t) cells.

This definition yields a time-varying frontier reflecting the most influential contemporaneous scientific advances in a field.
